Pleadings of the plaintiff: -
1.

This is a suit for permanent injunction filed by the plaintiff against the defendants whereby plaintiff has sought decree of permanent injunction thereby restraining the defendants from carrying out any demolition or dispossession of plaintiff in any manner from whatsoever in respect of plots bearing no.141 and 142 forming part of Khasra no.34 in Village Nangli Jalab, Abadi Krishna Park Extension, Delhi without due process of law.

2. The brief facts as mentioned in the plaint are that the plaintiff has been in exclusive physical possession of the residential plots bearing no. K-141, measuring 28x27.1/2 and K-142 measuring 28 and 36 respectively, forming part of Khasra no.34 in Village Nangli Jalab, Abadi Krishna Park Extension, Delhi, as general attorney of one Chote Lal S/o Sh. Richhpal, the owner thereof.
That the plaintiff had got constructed six shops in one row adjoining to each on Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-2/33 - 3 - the aforesaid plots bounded as below:-

That when on 22.06.1983, the officials of defendant illegally demolished the aforesaid shops in unauthorized manner without going through the process of law required in this respect in as much as the plaintiff or any of the said tenants never served with a show cause notice or a demolition order by the office of the defendant.

That, the plaintiff is contemplating to initiate legal proceeding for claiming damages from the defendants for having caused reckless demolition of the aforesaid shops situated on the aforesaid plots on 22.06.1983.
4.

That the plaintiff in his capacity as a General Attorney stands vested with the exclusive physical possession supervision, control and maintenance of the aforesaid property.
That the aforesaid demolition was carried on at the instance of some unscrupulous subordinate employees of the defendant who Suit No.1420/2018

OPP The onus to prove these issues was upon the plaintiff.

It is the case of the plaintiff that on 22.06.1983, the officials of DDA illegally demolished the 6 shops in question in an unauthorized manner without furnishing any show cause notice or demolition order to the plaintiff.

That to remedy the said grievance, the plaintiff had instituted the present suit,
thereby seeking restraining of the defendants from carrying out any demolition or dispossession of the plaintiff in any matter in respect to plot bearing no.K-141 and K-142, forming part of Khasra no.34, Village Nangli Jalab, abadi Krishna Park Extension, Delhi except without following the due process of law.
As such, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the present suit seeking the equitable remedy of permanent injunction against the alleged illegal and unauthorized action of DDA.
In this regard, it is pertinent to mention that the onus of proving the said issue is a strict one upon the plaintiff.
On the one hand, the grievance of the plaintiff is that DDA did not serve any notice on the plaintiff before conducting any demolition at the suit property on 23.06.1983.

While on the other hand, the stand of DDA is that no such alleged illegal Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-16/33 - 17 - action has been taken against the plaintiff rather the plaintiff has no right, title or interest in the suit property since the same has already been acquired vide award no.20/73-74 Ex.DW-1/1 (OSR) and the physical possession of the same has been handed over to DDA on 21.07.1973 Ex.DW-1/2 and as such the suit land has been placed at the disposal of DDA vide notification dated 25.09.1974 Ex.DW-1/3.

At this stage, it is further pertinent to mention that it is a matter of record in the present matter as well as in the writ petitions on similar issues filed before Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in WP(C)
313-19/2005 and 7370/2014 that the Khasra no.34 in Village Nangli Jalab, abadi Krishna Park Extension, was acquired by the government vide award Ex.DW-1/1 (OSR).

However, the concerned authorities were required to conduct a survey in light of the orders passed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the above said writ petition for taking of further action towards the development of outer ring road in accordance with law.

sentences.text: Due process of law means nobody ought to be condemned unheard.
The due process of law means a person in settled possession will not be dispossessed except by due process of law.
Due process means an opportunity for the Defendant to file pleadings including written statement and documents before the Court of law.
It does not mean the whole trial.
Due process of law is satisfied the moment rights of the parties are adjudicated by a competent Court.

82. The High Court of Delhi in a case Thomas Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-23/33 - 24 - Cook (India) Limited v. Hotel Imperial, 2006 (88) DRJ 545 : (AIR 2007) (NOC) 169)

"28 . The expressions 'due process of law', 'due course of law' and 'recourse to law'
have been interchangeably used in the decisions referred to above which say that the settled possession of even a person in unlawful possession cannot be disturbed 'forcibly' by the true owner taking law in his own hands.

All these expressions,
however, mean the same thing - ejectment from settled possession can only be had by recourse to a court of law.

Clearly, 'due process of law' or 'due course of law', here,
simply mean that a person in settled possession cannot be ejected without a court of law having adjudicated upon his rights qua the true owner.
Now, this 'due process' or 'due course' condition is satisfied the moment the rights of the parties are adjudicated upon by a court of competent jurisdiction.
It does not matter who brought the action to court.
It could be the owner in an action for enforcement of his right to eject the person in unlawful possession.
It could be the person who is sought to be ejected, in an action preventing the owner from ejecting him.

Whether the action is for enforcement of a right (recovery of possession) or protection of a right (injunction against dispossession), is not of much consequence."

However, this Court is of the opinion that the onus to prove this issue should have been upon DDA since the present issue has arisen from the preliminary objection taken by DDA in their written statement.
Nevertheless, the entirety of the evidence and pleadings of both the sides is required to be looked into.

It is the case of the plaintiff that on 22.06.1983, the officials of DDA illegally demolished the 6 shops in question in an unauthorized manner without furnishing any show cause notice or demolition order to the plaintiff.

That to remedy the said grievance, the plaintiff had instituted the present suit, thereby seeking restraining of the defendants from carrying out any demolition or dispossession of the plaintiff in any matter in respect to plot bearing no.141 and 142, forming part of Khasra no.34, Village Nangli Jalab, abadi Krishna Park Extension, Delhi except without following the due process of law.
As such, the present suit is one for seeking permanent injunction.

Before adverting further, let us first discuss Section 53B of the DDA Act, which reads as under:
"53B. Notice to be given of suits.--(1) No suit shall be instituted against the Authority,
or any member thereof, or any of its officers or other employees, or any person acting under the directions of the Authority or any member or any Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-29/33 - 30 - officer or other employee of the Authority in respect of any act done or purporting to have been done in pursuance of this Act or any rule or regulation made thereunder until the expiration of two months after notice in writing has been, in the case of the Authority, left at its office, and in any other case, delivered to, or left at the office or place of abode of, the person to be sued and unless such notice states explicitly the cause of action, the nature of relief sought, the amount of compensation claimed and the name and place of residence of the intending plaintiffs and unless the plaint contains a statement that such notice has been so left or delivered.
(2) No suit such as is described in sub-section (1) shall, unless it is a suit for recovery of immovable property or for a declaration of title thereto, be instituted after the expiry of six months from the date on which the cause of action arises.
(3) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) shall be deemed to apply to a suit in which the only relief claimed is an injunction of which the object would be defeated by the giving of the notice or the postponement of the institution of the suit.]"
[Emphasis Supplied] That, a bare reading of Section 53B of the DDA Act transpires that, the legislative intent behind such a provision is to ensure that, a government authority such as DDA is not entrapped in surprise litigations.

sentences.text: That the bare reading of Section 53B of the DDA Act further makes it evidently clear that the mandate of serving notice U/s 53B of DDA Act does not apply in the cases where the relief sought is of simplicitor permanent injunction.

The mischief behind the above said provision is that since permanent injunction is an equitable and emergent relief, therefore, in such circumstances the serving of notice upon DDA is not a sine qua non so that the ends of justice are not defeated and the suit be not rendered infructuous.
In the present matter as well, the plaintiff was aggrieved by the action of DDA in demolishing the suit property which was acting as a livelihood for the plaintiff.
Accordingly, the plaintiff was compelled to institute the present suit seeking the urgent and equitable remedy of injunction, so as to further safeguard his interest.
Accordingly, this Court is of the opinion that the plaintiff was not required to serve any notice to DDA before institution of the present suit U/s 53 B of DDA Act.
Hence, issue no. (4) is decided in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants.

That, the plaintiff has no locus standi to institute the present suit as neither the plaintiff is the owner nor has any legal right, concern or connection in the suit property.
That the suit property belongs to the government i.e. right of way of Road no.26 and a Park, therefore, the suit is not maintainable in the present form.
That the plaintiff is illegally occupying a Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-8/33 - 9 - government land and his status qua the property in dispute is only rank as trespasser, therefore, the plaintiff cannot be allowed to take the protection of the Court for his illegal act.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
That the suit does not disclose the cause of action, therefore,
the plaint is liable to be rejected U/O 7 Rule 11 CPC.
Fifthly,
plaintiff has grossly failed in cross-examining to the defence witnesses with respect to the alleged act of demolition and non-service of any notice.
Sixthly, that the plaintiff was in fact not even a party to the above said Writ Petitions and lastly, that the plaintiff has merely tried to benefit from the stay orders passed in the above said writ petitions and in garb of the same has tried to regain his possession by gathering the malba from the demolition site, without any right, title or interest.
Further,
the payment of any development or remittance charges paid by plaintiff at his own violation to DDA does not confer the plaintiff with any vested rights so much so the suit property of the plaintiff was being utilized as commercial shops and the regularization plan did not apply to it in the very first place.
Mrs.
Dharmi & Ors. Vs. State of Rajasthan [1992 WLN 305], Bhaskar Vs. State of Kerala [ILR 1995 KAR 183, Tuticorian New Shore Slum Dwellers Vs. The Chairman, Port Trust & Ors. [1991 95 MLJ 1].
That the crux of the law established in the above said judgment to the effect that any one in the settled possession even if a trespasser cannot be evicted from his property without following the Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-22/33 - 23 - due process of law.
In this regard, it is pertinent to mention that, however, the above said judgments have not laid down any straight jacket/blanket formula as to what will constitute due process of law, that is to say in terms of plaintiff- the defendant is required to institute a suit seeking possession.
82. The High Court of Delhi in a case Thomas Suit No.1420/2018 Narinder Singh Suri Vs. DDA & Ors. Page-23/33 - 24 - Cook (India) Limited v. Hotel Imperial, 2006 (88) DRJ 545 : (AIR 2007) (NOC) 169)
held as under:
In so far as the Trial Court's finding stating that DDA cannot dispossess the Plaintiffs without due process of law, is concerned, this is clearly an erroneous approach inasmuch as even if the Plaintiffs are stated to be in settled possession, it is not necessary for the DDA to file a suit to take possession from them.
The DDA can,
as a Defendant, establish before the Court that the Plaintiffs are in possession of a government land and the same can result in dismissal of the suit.
Due process of law, as is settled in several judgments of the Supreme Court and this Court, does not always require initiation of action by the owner/ Government.
Dismissal of a suit by a competent Court of law after affording proper opportunity to the parties, is also a recognized mode of following the due process of law.
As such, it cannot be said that due process of law has not been followed in the case of demolition or eviction of the plaintiff from the suit property.
Merely paying of development charges or remittance charges or remaining in symbolic possession by use of Malba at the demolition site in the garb of the stay orders, which were passed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi
,
already stood vacated vide order dated 07.10.2015, no right vests in the plaintiff whether in law or in equity.
Further, the plaintiff cannot reap benefit of non-conducting of the survey as per regularization plan or of fallacies in the case of the defence to seek any right, title or interest in the suit property, especially without challenging the acquisition proceedings and regularization plan and without seeking the appropriate relief of declaration of ownership.
That, the plaintiff was running commercial shops at the suit property and that the regularization plan applies only for residential purposes has been admitted by the plaintiff during his cross-examination.
Further, payment of any development charges per se does not vest any right, title or interest in the plaintiff in terms of the regularization plan, in so much so, the regularization plan is applicable only upon residential premises and not the commercial ones.
Thus defendant has been able to prove that the plaintiff has no locus standi to institute the present suit.
As such, the present suit is one for seeking permanent injunction.
That the bare reading of Section 53B of the DDA Act further makes it evidently clear that the mandate of serving notice U/s 53B of DDA Act does not apply in the cases where the relief sought is of simplicitor permanent injunction.
The mischief behind the above said provision is that since permanent injunction is an equitable and emergent relief, therefore, in such circumstances the serving of notice upon DDA is not a sine qua non so that the ends of justice are not defeated and the suit be not rendered infructuous.
In the present matter as well, the plaintiff was aggrieved by the action of DDA in demolishing the suit property which was acting as a livelihood for the plaintiff.
Accordingly, the plaintiff was compelled to institute the present suit seeking the urgent and equitable remedy of injunction, so as to further safeguard his interest.
